en: Theravāda Vinaya Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga Pācittiyakaṇḍa
Gabbhinīvagga 65.
The Training Rule on Married Women.
At that time the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the bhikkhunīs were ordaining women who had been married for less than twelve years.
They were unable to endure cold, heat, hunger, thirst, and contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping creatures; they were unable to endure harsh and offensive words;
and they were of a nature unable to tolerate arisen bodily feelings that were painful, racking, sharp, piercing, disagreeable, unpleasant, and life-threatening.
Those bhikkhunīs who were few in desires … [as above] … complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
“How can these bhikkhunīs give the full admission to a married girl who is less than twelve years old?
… [The Buddha asked: “Is it true, monks, that bhikkhunīs are giving the full admission to married girls who are less than twelve years old?”
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How can these bhikkhunīs, monks, give the full admission to a married girl who is less than twelve years old? This is not suitable, monks, for the training of the bhikkhunīs.”

“Monks, a woman who has gone to live with a householder and is less than twelve years old is unable to endure cold, heat, hunger, thirst, and contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things; she is unable to endure ill-spoken, unwelcome words from others;
and she is by nature unable to endure arisen bodily feelings that are painful, sharp, harsh, bitter, disagreeable, unpleasant, and life-threatening.”
“Monks, a woman who has gone forth as a householder is indeed able to endure cold, heat, hunger, thirst, and contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things;
she is able to endure ill-spoken, unwelcome words and physical sensations that have arisen—painful, sharp, harsh, bitter, disagreeable, unpleasant, and life-threatening.
Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence... [and so on].”
And furthermore, monks, the nuns should recite this training rule thus:
“Whichever nun, however, should give the full admission to a married girl who is less than twelve years old, that is an offense entailing expiation.
Whichever nun...
Whichever [nun], of whatever kind ... [pe] ... a bhikkhunī ...
[pe] ... this is the bhikkhunī intended in this context.
"Less than twelve years old" means not having reached twelve years of age.
"One who has gone to a householder's life" means...
"She who has gone over to another man" is what is said.
"Should ordain" means she should confer full admission.
If she seeks out a group, a preceptor, a bowl, or robes with the intention, “I will ordain her,” or if she demarcates a boundary, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
For the motion (ñatti), there is an offense of wrong-doing;
for two proclamations (kammavācā), there are offenses of wrong-doing.
At the conclusion of the formal ritual (kammavācā), the preceptor commits an offense of expiation (pācittiya);
the community and the instructor commit an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa).
If one who is less than twelve years [of seniority] ordains another while perceiving herself to be less than twelve years [of seniority], she commits an offense of expiation.
If she ordains one who is less than twelve years old while being in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If she ordains one who is less than twelve years old while perceiving her to be full [twelve], there is no offense.
If she ordains one who is full twelve years old while perceiving her to be less than twelve years old, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If she is more than twelve years old but she is in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If she is more than twelve years old and she perceives her as such, there is no offense.
There is no offense—
If she gives the full admission to one less than twelve years old while perceiving her to be full twelve years old,
or if she gives the full admission to one who is full twelve years old while perceiving her to be so,
or if she does so while insane;
"For one who is a first offender":
thus ends the fifth training rule.
